title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: At that very time, in circumstances even more significant than retreating without a battle — namely, the evacuation and burning of Moscow — Rostopchin, usually portrayed as the instigator of that event, acted in an entirely different manner from Kutuzov.
After the Battle of Borodino, the abandonment and burning of Moscow was as inevitable as the army's retreat beyond Moscow without fighting.
Every Russian could have predicted it — not through reasoning, but through the instinct planted in each of us and in our forebears.

The same thing that happened in Moscow had happened in every town and village on Russian soil from Smolensk onward, without any involvement from Count Rostopchin and his broadsheets. The people awaited the enemy calmly, without rioting or tearing anyone apart, but faced their fate with the inner strength to know what needed to be done at the most difficult moment. And as soon as the enemy drew near, the wealthy departed, abandoning their property, while the poor remained and burned and destroyed what was left.

The awareness that this would happen — that it would always happen — was and is present in the heart of every Russian. This awareness, this premonition that Moscow would be taken, existed in Moscow society in 1812. Those who had left the city already in July and early August showed they expected it. Those who departed, taking what they could and abandoning their homes and half their possessions, did so from a latent patriotism that expresses itself not through speeches or through giving up one's children to save the fatherland and similar unnatural gestures, but quietly, simply, organically — and therefore in the way that always produces the most powerful results.

"It is disgraceful to run from danger; only cowards are fleeing Moscow," they were told. In his broadsheets Rostopchin shamed them for leaving, insisting it was a disgrace. They were ashamed to be called cowards, ashamed to go — but they left anyway, knowing it had to be done. Why did they go? One can hardly suppose Rostopchin's horror stories about what Napoleon had done in conquered countries frightened them. The first to leave were the rich and educated, who knew perfectly well that Vienna and Berlin had remained intact, and that during Napoleon's occupation the residents had spent their time pleasantly in the company of charming Frenchmen, whom Russian women in particular found so appealing.

They left because for Russians there could be no question of whether things would go well or badly under French rule in Moscow. Being subject to French rule was out of the question — it would be the worst possible outcome. They left even before the Battle of Borodino, and even faster after it, despite Rostopchin's calls to defend Moscow, his announcement that he'd take the wonder-working icon of the Iberian Mother of God into battle, and his plans for hot-air balloons to destroy the French, and all the other nonsense he published in his broadsheets. They knew it was the army's job to fight, and if the army couldn't succeed, it made no sense to send young ladies and household servants to the Three Hills to fight Napoleon — they needed to leave, however sorry they were to abandon their property. They left without dwelling on the tremendous significance of a great city being handed over to destruction — for a great city of wooden buildings, once abandoned by its inhabitants, was certain to burn. Each left on his own account, and yet only because of their leaving was the momentous event accomplished that will always remain the greatest glory of the Russian people. The lady who, fearing she'd be stopped by Rostopchin's orders, had already moved to her Saratov estate in June with her household, with a vague sense that she was not Bonaparte's servant, was truly carrying out the great work that saved Russia. But Count Rostopchin — who now taunted those leaving, now had government offices evacuated; now distributed useless weapons to drunken mobs, now organized icon processions, now forbade Father Augustin to remove icons or holy relics; now seized all private carts in Moscow and used one hundred thirty-six of them to transport Leppich's balloon; now hinted he would burn Moscow and described setting fire to his own house; now published a proclamation solemnly scolding the French for destroying his orphanage; now claimed credit for suggesting Moscow be burned and now denied it; now ordered people to catch all spies and bring them to him, now reproached them for doing so; now expelled all French residents from Moscow, now let Madame Aubert-Chalme (the center of the entire French colony in Moscow) remain, while having the venerable old postmaster Klyucharev arrested and exiled for no particular offense; now assembled the people at the Three Hills to fight the French, and now, to be rid of them, handed over a man to be killed and himself slipped away by the back gate; now declared he would not survive Moscow's fall, now wrote French verses in albums about his role in the affair — this man did not understand the meaning of what was happening. He merely wanted to do something dramatic himself, to perform some patriotically heroic feat; and like a child he played games with the momentous, unavoidable event — the abandonment and burning of Moscow — and with his feeble hand tried now to speed, now to slow the enormous popular tide that carried him along.

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: Helene, having returned with the court from Vilna to Petersburg, found herself in a difficult position.

In Petersburg she had enjoyed the special protection of a grandee who held one of the highest posts in the Empire. In Vilna she had formed an intimate relationship with a young foreign prince. When she returned to Petersburg, both the magnate and the prince were there, and both claimed their rights. Helene was faced with a new problem — how to maintain her intimacy with both without offending either.

What would have seemed difficult or even impossible to another woman caused Countess Bezukhova not the slightest embarrassment, fully justifying her reputation as a very clever woman. Had she tried concealment or cunning to extricate herself from the awkward position, she would have undermined her case by admitting guilt. But Helene, like a truly great man who can do whatever he pleases, at once assumed her position to be perfectly correct — as she sincerely believed — and that everyone else was to blame.

The first time the young foreigner dared to reproach her, she lifted her beautiful head and, half turning to him, said firmly: "That's so typical of a man — selfish and cruel! I expected nothing better. A woman sacrifices herself for you, she suffers, and this is her reward! What right have you, monseigneur, to demand an account of my attachments and friendships? He is a man who has been more than a father to me!" The prince tried to say something, but Helene cut him off.

"Well, yes," she said, "perhaps he does have feelings for me beyond those of a father. But that is no reason for me to shut my door on him. I am not a man, to repay kindness with ingratitude! Know, monseigneur, that for everything concerning my intimate feelings, I answer only to God and to my conscience," she concluded, placing her hand on her beautiful, fully exposed bosom and gazing heavenward.
"But for heaven's sake, listen to me!"
"Marry me, and I will be your slave!"
"But that's impossible."
"You won't lower yourself to marry me, you..." said Helene, beginning to cry.

The prince tried to console her, but Helene, as if completely distraught, said through her tears that nothing prevented her from marrying, that there were precedents (there were very few at the time, but she mentioned Napoleon and some other eminent figures), that she had never been her husband's wife in the true sense, and that she had been sacrificed.
"But the law, religion..." said the prince, already yielding.
"The law, religion — what were they invented for if they can't sort this out?" said Helene.
The prince was surprised that so simple an idea hadn't occurred to him, and he consulted the holy brethren of the Society of Jesus, with whom he was on intimate terms.

A few days later, at one of those enchanting parties Helene gave at her country house on the Stone Island, the charming Monsieur de Jobert — a man no longer young, with snow-white hair and brilliant black eyes, a Jesuit in lay clothing — was introduced to her. In the garden, by the light of the illuminations and to the sound of music, he spoke to her at length about the love of God, of Christ, of the Sacred Heart, and of the consolations offered by the one true Catholic faith in this world and the next. Helene was moved, and more than once tears rose to her eyes and to Monsieur de Jobert's, and their voices trembled. A dance, for which her partner came to claim her, ended her discourse with her future spiritual director, but Monsieur de Jobert came to see Helene again the next evening when she was alone, and after that he visited often.
* A lay member of the Society of Jesus.

One day he took the countess to a Roman Catholic church, where she knelt before the altar to which she was led. The enchanting, middle-aged Frenchman laid his hands on her head and, as she herself later described it, she felt something like a fresh breeze waft into her soul. It was explained to her that this was grace.

After that, a long-robed abbe was brought to her. She confessed to him, and he absolved her of her sins. The next day she received a box containing the Sacred Host, left at her house for her to partake of. A few days later Helene learned with pleasure that she had been admitted to the true Catholic Church, and that soon the Pope himself would hear of her and would send her a certain document.

Everything done around her and to her at this time — the attention devoted to her by so many clever men, expressed in such pleasant, refined ways — and the state of dove-like purity she was now in (she wore only white dresses and white ribbons throughout) gave her pleasure. But this pleasure never for a moment distracted her from her goal. And as always happens in contests of cunning — that the stupid person outwits the clever ones — Helene, having understood that the real purpose of all these words and efforts was to convert her to Catholicism in order to extract money for Jesuit institutions (she had received hints of this), insisted before parting with any money that the various steps necessary to free her from her husband should be taken. In her view, the purpose of any religion was simply to maintain certain proprieties while satisfying human desires. And with this aim, in one of her conversations with her confessor, she demanded an answer to the question: to what extent was she bound by her marriage?

They were sitting in the twilight by a window in the drawing room. The scent of flowers drifted in through the window. Helene wore a white dress, transparent at the shoulders and bosom. The abbe — a well-fed man with a plump, clean-shaven chin, a pleasant firm mouth, and white hands meekly folded on his knees — sat close to Helene. With a subtle smile on his lips and a peaceful look of delight at her beauty, he occasionally glanced at her face as he explained his views on the matter. Helene, with an uneasy smile, looked at his curly hair and his plump, clean-shaven, dark-stubbled cheeks, expecting at every moment the conversation to take a new turn. But the abbe, though clearly enjoying his companion's beauty, was absorbed in his mastery of the argument.

The Father Confessor's argument ran as follows: "Ignorant of what you were undertaking, you made a vow of marital fidelity to a man who, for his part, by entering marriage without faith in its religious significance, committed an act of sacrilege. That marriage therefore lacked the dual meaning it should have had. Yet despite this, your vow was binding. You broke it. In doing so, did you commit a venial or a mortal sin? A venial sin, because you acted without evil intent. If you now married again for the purpose of bearing children, your sin could be forgiven. But the question is again twofold: first..."

But suddenly Helene, who was getting bored, said with one of her bewitching smiles: "But I think that since I have embraced the true religion, I cannot be bound by obligations imposed by a false one."

The spiritual director was astonished at having the case presented with the simplicity of Columbus's egg. He was delighted at his pupil's rapid progress but could not abandon the edifice of argument he had so laboriously constructed.
"Let us understand one another, Countess," he said with a smile, and began refuting his spiritual daughter's arguments.

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: Helene understood that the question was quite simple from the Church's point of view, and that her spiritual directors were creating difficulties only because they feared how the secular authorities would react.

So she decided to prepare public opinion. She provoked the jealousy of the elderly magnate and told him what she had told the other suitor — that the only way for him to have a claim on her was to marry her. The elderly magnate was at first just as startled by the suggestion of marrying a woman whose husband was still alive as the younger man had been, but Helene's unshakable conviction that it was as simple and natural as marrying a single woman had its effect on him too. Had Helene herself shown the slightest sign of hesitation, shame, or secrecy, her cause would certainly have been lost; but not only did she show no such signs — on the contrary, with good-natured openness she told her close friends (which meant all of Petersburg) that both the prince and the magnate had proposed, and that she loved both and was afraid of hurting either.

A rumor immediately spread through Petersburg — not that Helene wanted to divorce her husband (had such a report spread, many would have opposed so illegal an intention), but simply that the unfortunate and fascinating Helene was torn over which of the two men to marry. The question was no longer whether this was permissible, but only which was the better match and how the court would view it. There were, admittedly, some rigid individuals who could not rise to such heights and who saw the whole scheme as a desecration of the sacrament of marriage, but there weren't many, and they kept quiet. The majority were interested in Helene's good fortune and in the question of which match would be more advantageous. Whether it was right or wrong to remarry while one's husband was living, they did not discuss — that question had obviously been settled by people "wiser than you or me," as they said, and to doubt that decision was to risk exposing one's own stupidity and inability to function in society.

Only Marya Dmitrievna Akhrosimova, who had come to Petersburg that summer to visit one of her sons, allowed herself to express an opinion contrary to the general one. Meeting Helene at a ball, she stopped her in the middle of the room and, amid general silence, said in her gruff voice: "So wives of living men have started marrying again! Maybe you think you've invented something new? You've been beaten to it, my dear! It was thought of long ago. It's done in all the brothels." And with those words, Marya Dmitrievna rolled up her wide sleeves with her usual threatening gesture, glanced sternly around, and marched across the room.

Though people feared Marya Dmitrievna, she was regarded in Petersburg as a buffoon, and of what she'd said they noticed and repeated in whispers only the one crude word she'd used, assuming the entire sting of her remark lay in it.
Prince Vasily, who lately often forgot what he'd said and repeated the same thing a hundred times, remarked to his daughter whenever he happened to see her:

"Helene, I have something to say to you," and he would lead her aside, drawing her hand downward. "I've heard about certain plans concerning... you know. Well, my dear child, you know how your father's heart rejoices to know that you... You have suffered so much. But, my dear child, consult only your own heart. That is all I have to say." And concealing his invariable emotion, he would press his cheek to his daughter's and move away.

Bilibin, who had not lost his reputation as an exceedingly clever man, and who was one of the disinterested male friends that a brilliant woman like Helene always has — friends who can never become lovers — once gave her his view of the matter at a small, private gathering.

"Listen, Bilibin," said Helene (she always called such friends by their last names), touching his coat sleeve with her white, ring-laden fingers. "Tell me, as you would a sister, what I should do. Which of the two?"
Bilibin wrinkled the skin over his eyebrows and thought, smiling.

"You're not catching me off guard, you know," he said. "As a true friend, I've thought and thought about your situation. You see, if you marry the prince" — he meant the younger man, and he crooked one finger — "you lose forever the chance of marrying the other, and you'll displease the court besides. (You know there's some sort of connection.) But if you marry the old count, you'll make his last days happy, and as a widow of the Grand... the prince would no longer be making a poor match by marrying you." And Bilibin smoothed out his forehead.

"That's what a true friend sounds like!" said Helene, beaming, and she touched Bilibin's sleeve again. "But I love them both, you know, and I don't want to hurt either. I would give my life for the happiness of both."
Bilibin shrugged, as if to say that not even he could help with that.
"A masterly woman! That's what's called having it all figured out. She'd like to marry all three at once," he thought.
* A masterly woman.
"But tell me, how will your husband view the matter?" Bilibin asked — his reputation was so well established that he didn't fear asking so blunt a question. "Will he agree?"
"Oh, he loves me so!" said Helene, who for some reason imagined that Pierre too loved her. "He'll do anything for me."
Bilibin pursed his lips in preparation for something witty.
"Even divorce you?" he said.
Helene laughed.

Among those who dared to question the legitimacy of the proposed marriage was Helene's mother, Princess Kuragina. She was constantly tormented by jealousy of her daughter, and now that the jealousy concerned a subject close to her own heart, she couldn't accept the idea. She consulted a Russian priest about the possibility of divorce and remarriage during a husband's lifetime, and the priest told her it was impossible, and to her delight showed her a Gospel passage that (as he saw it) plainly forbids remarriage while the husband lives.
Armed with these arguments, which seemed to her unanswerable, she went to her daughter's early one morning to catch her alone.
Having listened to her mother's objections, Helene smiled blandly and ironically.
"But it says clearly: 'Whosoever shall marry her that is divorced...'" said the old princess.

"Oh, Mama, don't talk nonsense. You don't understand anything. In my position I have obligations," Helene said, switching from Russian — in which she always felt her case didn't sound quite right — to French, which suited it better.
* "Oh, Mama, don't talk nonsense. You don't understand anything. In my position I have obligations."
"But, my dear..."
"Oh, Mama, how can you not understand that the Holy Father, who has the right to grant dispensations..."
Just then the companion who lived with Helene came in to announce that His Highness was in the ballroom and wished to see her.
"No, tell him I don't wish to see him. I am furious with him for not keeping his word to me."
* "No, tell him I don't wish to see him. I am furious with him for not keeping his word to me."
"Countess, there is mercy for every sin," said a fair-haired young man with a long face and nose as he entered the room.
* "Countess, there is mercy for every sin."
The old princess rose respectfully and curtsied. The young man who had entered took no notice of her. The princess nodded to her daughter and sidled out of the room.

"Yes, she is right," the old princess thought, all her convictions dissolving at the sight of His Highness. "She is right — but how is it that we, in our irrecoverable youth, didn't know it? Yet it is so simple," she mused as she got into her carriage.

By the beginning of August, Helene's plans were clearly defined, and she wrote a letter to her husband — who, she imagined, loved her very much — informing him of her intention to marry N.N. and of her conversion to the one true faith, and asking him to complete the formalities necessary for a divorce, which would be explained to him by the letter's bearer.
And so I pray God to have you, my friend, in His holy and powerful keeping — Your friend Helene.
This letter was delivered to Pierre's house while he was on the field of Borodino.

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: Toward the end of the Battle of Borodino, Pierre — having run down from Raevsky's battery a second time — made his way through a gully to Knyazkovo with a crowd of soldiers, reached the dressing station, and seeing blood and hearing cries and groans, hurried on, still caught up in the stream of soldiers.

The one thing he now wanted with his whole soul was to get away quickly from the terrible experiences of that day and return to ordinary life — to sleep peacefully in a room, in his own bed. He felt that only under normal conditions would he be able to make sense of himself and everything he had seen and felt. But such normal conditions were nowhere to be found.

Though shells and bullets no longer whistled over the road he was traveling, on all sides there was the same thing as on the battlefield — the same suffering, exhausted, and sometimes strangely indifferent faces, the same blood, the same soldiers' overcoats, the same sounds of firing that, though distant now, still inspired terror — and in addition the foul air and the dust.
After walking a couple of miles along the Mozhaysk road, Pierre sat down by the roadside.

Dusk had fallen and the roar of guns died away. Pierre lay propped on his elbow for a long time, watching the shadows pass him in the darkness. He kept imagining a cannonball flying toward him with a terrifying whistle — then he would shudder and sit up. He had no idea how long he'd been there. In the middle of the night, three soldiers who had gathered firewood settled near him and began lighting a fire.

The soldiers, casting sideways glances at Pierre, got the fire going and set an iron pot on it, into which they broke some dried bread and added a little fat. The pleasant smell of greasy food mixed with the scent of smoke. Pierre sat up and sighed. The three soldiers were eating and talking among themselves, paying him no attention.

"And who might you be?" one of them suddenly asked Pierre, clearly meaning what Pierre himself had been thinking — namely: "If you want to eat, we'll give you some food, only let us know whether you're an honest man."

"I... I'm..." said Pierre, feeling it necessary to minimize his social standing so as to be closer to the soldiers and better understood by them. "Technically I'm a militia officer, but my men aren't here. I came to the battle and got separated from them."
"Well, well!" said one of the soldiers.
Another shook his head.
"Would you like a little mash?" the first soldier asked, handing Pierre a wooden spoon after licking it clean.

Pierre sat down by the fire and began eating the mash — as they called the food in the pot — and thought it was the most delicious thing he had ever tasted. As he bent greedily over it, scooping up large spoonfuls one after another, his face was lit by the firelight and the soldiers watched him in silence.
"Where do you need to go? Tell us!" said one of them.
"To Mozhaysk."
"You're a gentleman, aren't you?"
"Yes."
"And what's your name?"
"Peter Kirilych."
"Well then, Peter Kirilych, come along with us — we'll get you there."
In the total darkness the soldiers walked with Pierre to Mozhaysk.

By the time they neared Mozhaysk and began climbing the steep hill into town, the roosters were already crowing. Pierre walked on with the soldiers, completely forgetting that his inn was at the bottom of the hill and that he'd already passed it. He wouldn't have remembered this at all, so deep was his state of abstraction, had he not stumbled halfway up the hill upon his groom, who had been looking for him in town and was heading back to the inn. The groom recognized Pierre in the darkness by his white hat.
"Your excellency!" he said. "We were starting to despair! How is it you're on foot? And where are you going?"
"Oh, yes!" said Pierre.
The soldiers stopped.
"So you've found your people?" said one of them. "Well, goodbye, Peter Kirilych — isn't it?"
"Goodbye, Peter Kirilych!" Pierre heard the other voices repeat.
"Goodbye!" he said, and turned with his groom toward the inn.
"I ought to give them something!" he thought, reaching into his pocket. "No, better not," said another, inner voice.
There was no room to be had at the inn — they were all occupied. Pierre went out into the yard and, covering himself from head to toe, lay down in his carriage.

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: Pierre had barely laid his head on the pillow before he felt himself falling asleep, but suddenly — with almost the vividness of reality — he heard the boom, boom, boom of firing, the thud of projectiles, groans and cries, and smelled blood and powder, and a feeling of horror and dread of death seized him. He opened his eyes in fright and lifted his head from under his cloak. Everything in the yard was peaceful. Only someone's orderly splashed through the mud at the gate, chatting with the innkeeper. Above Pierre's head, some pigeons — disturbed by his movement — fluttered under the dark roof of the shed. The whole courtyard was filled with a strong, peaceful smell of stables, which Pierre found delightful at that moment. He could see the clear, starry sky between the dark roofs of two sheds.

"Thank God — no more of that!" he thought, pulling the cloak back over his head. "Oh, what a terrible thing fear is, and how shamefully I gave in to it! But they... they were steady and calm to the very end..." he thought.

They, in Pierre's mind, were the soldiers — those at the battery, those who had given him food, those who had prayed before the icon. They — those strange men he hadn't known before — stood out sharply and clearly from everyone else.

"To be a soldier, just a common soldier!" Pierre thought as he fell asleep. "To merge completely into that communal life, to be filled with whatever makes them who they are. But how do you shed all the superfluous, devilish burden of the outer man? There was a time I could have done it. I could have run away from my father, as I wanted to. Or I might have been sent into the army after the duel with Dolokhov." And the memory of the dinner at the English Club, when he had challenged Dolokhov, flashed through his mind, and then he remembered his benefactor at Torzhok. And now he pictured a solemn Masonic meeting at the English Club, and someone dear and familiar sat at the end of the table. "Yes, that's him! My benefactor. But he died!" thought Pierre. "Yes, he died, and I didn't know he was alive. How sorry I am that he died, and how glad I am that he's alive again!" On one side of the table sat Anatole, Dolokhov, Nesvitsky, Denisov, and others like them (in his dream this category was as clearly defined as the category he called they), and he heard those people — Anatole and Dolokhov — shouting and singing loudly; yet through their noise, the voice of his benefactor could be heard speaking continuously, and the sound of his words was as weighty and unbroken as the booming on the battlefield, but pleasant and comforting. Pierre couldn't make out what his benefactor was saying, but knew (the categories of thought were perfectly distinct in the dream) that he was speaking of goodness and the possibility of being what they were. And they, with their simple, kind, firm faces, surrounded his benefactor on all sides. But though they were kindly, they didn't look at Pierre and didn't know him. Wanting to speak and draw their attention, he started to rise, but at that moment his legs grew cold and bare.

He felt embarrassed, and with one arm covered his legs from which his cloak had in fact slipped. For a moment, as he adjusted it, Pierre opened his eyes and saw the same shed roofs, posts, and yard, but now everything was tinged with blue, sparkling with frost or dew.

"It's dawn," Pierre thought. "But that's not what I want. I want to hear and understand my benefactor's words." He pulled the cloak over himself again, but now neither the lodge nor his benefactor was there. Only thoughts remained — thoughts clearly expressed in words, thoughts that someone was saying or that he himself was forming.

Afterward, when he recalled those thoughts, Pierre was convinced they had been spoken by someone outside himself, though the impressions of that day had prompted them. He had never, it seemed to him, been able to think and express his thoughts so clearly when awake.

"To endure war is the most difficult submission of human freedom to the law of God," the voice had said. "Simplicity is submission to the will of God; you cannot escape Him. And they are simple. They don't talk — they act. The spoken word is silver, but the unspoken word is golden. Man can master nothing while he fears death, but he who does not fear it possesses everything. If there were no suffering, man would not know his limits — would not know himself. The hardest thing" — Pierre went on thinking, or hearing, in his dream — "is to unite in your soul the meaning of everything. To unite everything?" he asked himself. "No, not unite. You can't unite thoughts. But to harness all these thoughts together — that is what we need! Yes, harness them — harness them!" he repeated to himself with inner ecstasy, feeling that these words alone expressed what he wanted to say and solved the question that tormented him.
"Yes, one must harness — it is time to harness."
"Time to harness, time to harness, your excellency! Your excellency!" a voice kept repeating. "We must harness — it is time to harness..."

It was the voice of the groom, trying to wake him. The sun shone straight into Pierre's face. He glanced at the dirty inn yard where soldiers were watering their thin horses at the pump while carts passed out through the gate. Pierre turned away with distaste and, closing his eyes, quickly fell back onto the carriage seat. "No, I don't want that — I don't want to see and understand that. I want to understand what was being revealed to me in my dream. One more second and I would have grasped it all! But what should I do? Harness — but how can I harness everything?" And Pierre felt with horror that the meaning of everything he had seen and thought in the dream was crumbling away.
The groom, the coachman, and the innkeeper told Pierre that an officer had come with news that the French were already near Mozhaysk and that the Russian forces were leaving the town.
Pierre got up and, telling them to harness the horses and overtake him, set off on foot through the town.

The troops were moving out, leaving about ten thousand wounded behind. Wounded men were visible in the yards, at the windows of houses, and the streets were packed with them. In the streets, around the carts that were to carry some of the wounded away, shouts, curses, and blows could be heard. Pierre offered his carriage, which had caught up with him, to a wounded general he knew, and drove with him to Moscow. On the way, Pierre learned of the deaths of his brother-in-law Anatole and of Prince Andrew.

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: On August 30, Pierre reached Moscow. Near the city gates he was met by Count Rostopchin's adjutant.
"We've been looking for you everywhere," said the adjutant. "The count wants to see you urgently. He asks you to come at once on a very important matter."
Without going home, Pierre took a cab and drove to see the Moscow commander in chief.

Count Rostopchin had returned to town from his summer villa at Sokolniki only that morning. The anteroom and reception room of his house were full of officials who had been summoned or had come for instructions. Vasilchikov and Platov had already met with the count and explained that it was impossible to defend Moscow — it would have to be surrendered. Though this news was being kept from the residents, the officials — the heads of the various government departments — knew that Moscow would soon fall to the enemy, just as Rostopchin himself knew it. To avoid personal responsibility, they had all come to the governor to ask how to handle their departments.
As Pierre was entering the reception room, a courier from the army came out of Rostopchin's private room.
In answer to the questions people fired at him, the courier made a despairing gesture with his hand and passed through the room.

While waiting in the reception room, Pierre watched the various officials — old and young, military and civilian — with weary eyes. They all seemed dissatisfied and uneasy. Pierre approached a group of men, one of whom he knew. After greeting Pierre, they continued their conversation.
"If they're sent away and brought back later, no harm done — but as things stand now, nobody can guarantee anything."
"But look at what he writes..." said another, pointing to a printed sheet in his hand.
"That's a different matter. That's meant for the people," said the first.
"What is it?" asked Pierre.
"Oh, another broadsheet."
Pierre took it and began reading.

His Serene Highness has passed through Mozhaysk to join up with the troops moving toward him and has taken up a strong position where the enemy won't attack soon. Forty-eight guns with ammunition have been sent to him from here, and his Serene Highness says he will defend Moscow to the last drop of blood and is even prepared to fight in the streets. Don't worry, brothers — the courts are closed because things need to be put in order, and we'll deal with the criminals our own way! When the time comes I'll call for both townsmen and peasant lads, and I'll raise the cry a day or two beforehand — but they're not needed yet, so I'm holding my tongue. An ax will do nicely, a hunting spear isn't bad, but a three-pronged pitchfork is best of all: a Frenchman is no heavier than a sheaf of rye. Tomorrow after dinner I'll take the Iberian icon of the Mother of God to the wounded at the Catherine Hospital, where we'll bless some water. That will help them get well quicker. I'm well now too — one eye was sore but now I'm keeping watch with both.
"But military men have told me it's impossible to fight in the city," said Pierre, "and that the position..."
"Of course! That's exactly what we were saying," replied the first speaker.
"And what does he mean by 'One eye was sore but now I'm watching with both'?" asked Pierre.

"The count had a sty," the adjutant replied, smiling, "and was very upset when I told him people had been asking what was wrong with him. By the way, Count," he added suddenly, turning to Pierre with a smile, "we hear you have family troubles — that the countess, your wife..."
"I haven't heard anything," Pierre replied indifferently. "But what have you heard?"
"Oh, well, you know how people invent things. I'm only saying what I heard."
"But what did you hear?"
"Well, they say," the adjutant continued with the same smile, "that the countess, your wife, is preparing to go abroad. I'm sure it's nonsense..."
"Possibly," Pierre remarked, looking around absently. "And who is that?" he asked, indicating a short old man in a clean blue peasant coat, with a big snow-white beard and eyebrows and a ruddy face.
"Him? That's a tradesman — the restaurant keeper, Vereshchagin. Maybe you've heard about that business with the proclamation."
"Oh, so that's Vereshchagin!" said Pierre, studying the firm, calm face of the old man and looking for any sign that he might be a traitor.
"That's not the man himself — that's the father of the one who wrote the proclamation," said the adjutant. "The young man is in prison, and I expect things will go badly for him."
An old gentleman wearing a decoration and another official, a German with a cross around his neck, approached the speaker.

"It's a complicated story, you know," said the adjutant. "That proclamation appeared about two months ago. The count was informed and ordered an investigation. Gabriel Ivanovich here made the inquiries. The proclamation had passed through exactly sixty-three hands. He'd ask one person, 'Where did you get it?' — 'From so-and-so.' He'd go to the next — 'Where did you get it?' — and so on until he reached Vereshchagin, a half-educated tradesman, 'a pet of a merchant,' as they say." The adjutant smiled. "They asked him, 'Who gave it to you?' Now the point is, we knew who'd given it to him. He could only have gotten it from the Postmaster. But evidently they'd made some arrangement. He answered: 'From nobody — I wrote it myself.' They threatened and questioned him, but he stuck to his story: 'I wrote it myself.' And so it was reported to the count, who sent for the man. 'Where did you get the proclamation?' — 'I wrote it myself.' Well, you know the count," the adjutant said cheerfully, smiling with pride, "he flew into a terrible rage — just imagine the man's audacity, lying and stubbornness!"
"And the count wanted him to say it came from Klyucharev? I see!" said Pierre.

"Not at all!" the adjutant replied in dismay. "Klyucharev had his own sins to answer for, which is why he was banished. But the point is, the count was furious. 'How could you have written it yourself?' he said, and he grabbed the Hamburg Gazette lying on the table. 'Here it is! You didn't write it — you translated it, and translated it wretchedly, because you don't even know French, you fool!' And what do you think? 'No,' says the man, 'I haven't read any newspapers — I made it up myself.' 'If that's so, you're a traitor and I'll have you tried and hanged! Tell me who gave it to you.' 'I haven't seen any papers — I made it up myself.' And that was the end of it. The count had the father brought in, but the son stuck to his story. He was sent to trial and sentenced to hard labor, I believe. Now the father has come to plead for him. But he's a worthless fellow! You know the type — a tradesman's son, a dandy and ladies' man. He attended some lectures somewhere and thinks the devil himself is no match for him. That's the kind of fellow he is. His father runs a cookshop here by the Stone Bridge, and you know there was a large icon of God Almighty painted with a scepter in one hand and an orb in the other. Well, he took that icon home for a few days, and what did he do? He found some scoundrel of a painter..."

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: In the middle of this story Pierre was summoned to the commander in chief.

When he entered the private room, Count Rostopchin — his face scrunched up — was rubbing his forehead and eyes with his hand. A short man was saying something, but when Pierre came in, he stopped and left.

"Ah, hello there, great warrior!" said Rostopchin as soon as the short man had gone. "We've heard about your heroics. But that's not why you're here. Between us, my friend — are you a Mason?" He went on sternly, as though there were something wrong with it that he nevertheless intended to overlook. Pierre said nothing. "I am well informed, my friend, but I know there are Masons and Masons, and I hope you are not one of those who, under the pretense of saving mankind, wish to ruin Russia."
"Yes, I am a Mason," Pierre replied.

"There, you see, my friend! I expect you know that Messrs. Speransky and Magnitsky have been sent where they belong. Mr. Klyucharev has been treated the same way, and so have others who, under the guise of building Solomon's Temple, have tried to destroy the temple of their fatherland. You can understand there are reasons for this, and I could not have exiled the Postmaster had he not been a dangerous man. It has now come to my knowledge that you lent him your carriage for his departure from the city, and that you even took papers from him for safekeeping. I like you and don't wish you any harm, and since you're only half my age, I advise you as a father would: cut off all contact with people of that kind and leave here as soon as possible."
"But what did Klyucharev do wrong, Count?" asked Pierre.
"That is for me to know, not for you to ask!" Rostopchin shouted.
"If he is accused of distributing Napoleon's proclamation, it hasn't been proved," said Pierre, not looking at Rostopchin, "and Vereshchagin..."

"There we are!" Rostopchin shouted at Pierre even louder than before, scowling. "Vereshchagin is a renegade and a traitor who will be punished as he deserves," he said with the vindictive heat people show when recalling an insult. "But I didn't summon you to discuss my actions. I summoned you to give you advice — or an order, if you prefer. I ask you to leave the city and sever all ties with people like Klyucharev. And I'll knock the nonsense out of anyone" — but probably realizing he was shouting at Bezukhov, who so far wasn't guilty of anything, he added, taking Pierre's hand in a friendly way — "We're on the eve of a public catastrophe and I haven't time to be polite to everyone who has business with me. My head is spinning sometimes. Well, my friend, what are you doing personally?"
"Nothing," answered Pierre, without raising his eyes or changing his thoughtful expression.
The count frowned.

"A word of friendly advice, my friend: get out of here as soon as you can — that's all I have to say. A word to the wise. Goodbye, my dear fellow. Oh, by the way!" he shouted through the doorway after Pierre. "Is it true that the countess has fallen into the clutches of the Jesuits?"
Pierre did not answer and left Rostopchin's room more sullen and angry than he had ever shown himself.

When he reached home it was already getting dark. About eight people had come to see him that evening: the secretary of a committee, the colonel of his battalion, his steward, his major-domo, and various petitioners. They all had business with Pierre and needed decisions. Pierre didn't understand any of their questions and wasn't interested in them; he answered only to get rid of these people. When finally left alone, he opened and read his wife's letter.

"They — the soldiers at the battery, Prince Andrew killed... that old man... Simplicity is submission to God. Suffering is necessary... the meaning of everything... one must harness... my wife is getting married... One must forget and understand..." And going to his bed he threw himself on it without undressing and instantly fell asleep.

When he woke the next morning, the major-domo came to tell him that a special messenger — a police officer — had come from Count Rostopchin to find out whether Count Bezukhov had left or was leaving the city.
A dozen people with business were waiting for Pierre in the drawing room. He dressed hurriedly and, instead of going to see them, went to the back porch and out through the gate.
From that time until the end of Moscow's destruction, none of the Bezukhov household — despite all their searching — saw Pierre again or knew where he was.

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: The Rostovs remained in Moscow until September 1 — the eve of the enemy's entry into the city.

After Petya had joined Obolensky's Cossack regiment and left for Belaya Tserkov where the regiment was forming, the countess was seized with terror. The thought that both her sons were at war — that both had left the safety of her wing, and that today or tomorrow either or both might be killed, as the three sons of one of her acquaintances had been — struck her that summer for the first time with cruel clarity. She tried to get Nicholas sent home and wanted to go herself to fetch Petya, or to get him assigned somewhere in Petersburg, but neither proved possible. Petya couldn't return unless his regiment did, or unless he was transferred to another active unit. Nicholas was somewhere with the army and hadn't written since his last letter, which gave a detailed account of his meeting with Princess Mary. The countess couldn't sleep at night, and when she did she dreamed of her sons lying dead. After many consultations, the count devised a way to calm her: he got Petya transferred from Obolensky's regiment to Bezukhov's, which was training near Moscow. Though Petya would remain in service, this transfer gave the countess the consolation of having at least one son within reach, and she hoped to arrange things so he'd never be sent to battle again. As long as only Nicholas was in danger, the countess imagined she loved her firstborn more than all her other children and even reproached herself for it; but when her youngest — the scapegrace who'd been bad at lessons, always breaking things and annoying everyone, that snub-nosed Petya with his cheerful black eyes and fresh rosy cheeks where soft fuzz was just beginning to show — when he was thrown among those big, terrible, cruel men who were fighting somewhere about something and apparently enjoying it, then his mother felt she loved him more, much more, than all the rest. The nearer the time came for Petya to return, the more anxious the countess grew. She began to think she would never live to see such happiness. The presence of Sonya, of beloved Natasha, or even of her husband irritated her. "What do I need them for? I need no one but Petya," she thought.

At the end of August the Rostovs received another letter from Nicholas. He wrote from the province of Voronezh, where he'd been sent to procure horses, but the letter did not ease the countess. Knowing one son was out of danger only made her more anxious about Petya.

Although by the twentieth of August nearly all the Rostovs' acquaintances had left Moscow, and everyone urged the countess to leave as quickly as possible, she refused to hear of going before her treasure — her adored Petya — returned. On August 28 he arrived. The passionate tenderness with which his mother received him displeased the sixteen-year-old officer. Though she hid from him her plan to keep him close, Petya guessed her intentions and, instinctively fearing that he might give in to emotion with her — might "go soft," as he put it to himself — he treated her coolly, avoided her, and during his stay in Moscow attached himself exclusively to Natasha, for whom he had always had an especially brotherly, almost lover-like tenderness.

Due to the count's habitual carelessness, nothing was ready for departure by August 28, and the carts that were supposed to come from their Ryazan and Moscow estates to carry away their belongings didn't arrive until the thirtieth.

From the twenty-eighth to the thirty-first, all Moscow was in an uproar. Every day thousands of men wounded at Borodino were brought in through the Dorogomilov gate and taken to various parts of the city, and thousands of carts carried residents and their possessions out through the other gates. Despite Rostopchin's broadsheets — or because of them, or independently of them — the wildest and most contradictory rumors circulated. Some said no one would be allowed to leave; others said all the icons had been removed from the churches and everyone would be ordered to go. Some claimed another battle after Borodino had routed the French, while others insisted the Russian army had been destroyed. Some talked about the Moscow militia marching to the Three Hills led by the clergy; others whispered that Father Augustin had been forbidden to leave, that traitors had been caught, that peasants were rioting and robbing people on the roads out of Moscow, and so on. But all this was only talk; in reality — though the Council of Fili, at which it was decided to abandon Moscow, had not yet been held — both those who left and those who stayed felt, though they didn't show it, that Moscow would certainly be given up and that they should get away as quickly as possible. Everyone sensed that everything would suddenly collapse and change, but through September 1 nothing had. Like a condemned man being led to execution who looks around and straightens the crooked cap on his head, Moscow involuntarily continued its usual life, though it knew the time of its destruction was near — when the conditions its people were accustomed to would be completely overturned.

During the three days before the occupation, the entire Rostov family was absorbed in various activities. The head of the family, Count Ilya Rostov, drove about the city constantly, collecting rumors from all sides and issuing hasty, confused orders at home about preparations for departure.

The countess watched the packing, was dissatisfied with everything, was constantly chasing after Petya — who kept running away from her — and was jealous of Natasha, with whom he spent all his time. Sonya alone handled the practical side, getting things packed. But lately Sonya had been particularly sad and quiet. Nicholas's letter, in which he mentioned Princess Mary, had prompted joyful comments from the countess — made in Sonya's presence — about seeing Providence at work in bringing the princess and Nicholas together.

"I was never pleased about Bolkonsky's engagement to Natasha," said the countess, "but I always wanted Nicholas to marry the princess, and had a feeling it would happen. What a good match it would be!"

Sonya felt this was true — that the only way to restore the Rostov family's finances was for Nicholas to marry a wealthy woman, and that the princess was an excellent match. It was very bitter for her. But despite her grief — or perhaps because of it — she took on all the difficult work of organizing the packing and was busy all day long. The count and countess turned to her whenever orders needed giving. Petya and Natasha, by contrast, were generally a nuisance and a hindrance. Nearly all day the house rang with their running feet, their shouts, and their spontaneous laughter. They laughed and were joyful not because there was any reason to be, but because gladness and mirth filled their hearts and so everything that happened gave them cause for laughter. Petya was in high spirits because having left home a boy he had returned — as everyone told him — a fine young man; because he was at home; because he'd left Belaya Tserkov where there was no hope of seeing battle anytime soon and had come to Moscow where there would be fighting any day; and chiefly because Natasha, whose lead he always followed, was in high spirits. Natasha was gay because she had been sad too long and now nothing reminded her of the cause of her sadness, and because she was feeling well. She was also happy because she had someone to adore her — the adoration of others was the lubricant her machinery needed to run smoothly, and Petya adored her. Above all, they were gay because there was a war near Moscow, there would be fighting at the city gates, weapons were being handed out, everyone was escaping and going somewhere, and in general something extraordinary was happening — and that is always exciting, especially to the young.

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: Madame Schoss, who had been visiting her daughter, increased the countess's fears still further by describing what she'd seen at a liquor shop on Myasnitsky Street. Returning by that street, she'd been unable to pass because of a drunken crowd rioting in front of the shop. She'd taken a cab and gone home by a side street, and the cabman told her the people were smashing open the barrels at the drink store, having been given orders to do so.

After dinner the whole Rostov household set to work with feverish haste packing and preparing for departure. The old count, suddenly leaping into action, kept rushing between the yard and the house, shouting confused instructions and making everyone even more flustered. Petya took charge in the yard. Sonya, overwhelmed by the count's contradictory orders, lost her bearings entirely. The servants ran noisily through the house and yard, shouting and arguing. Natasha, with the fierce determination she brought to everything, threw herself into the work too. At first her involvement was met with skepticism — everyone expected some prank and didn't want to obey her. But she resolutely and passionately demanded compliance, grew angry, nearly cried because they wouldn't listen, and finally made them trust her. Her first feat — which took enormous effort and established her authority — was the packing of the carpets. The count owned valuable Gobelin tapestries and Persian carpets. When Natasha started, two cases stood open in the ballroom — one nearly full of crockery, the other of carpets. There was also a great deal of china on the tables, with more being brought from the storeroom. A third case was needed, and servants had gone to fetch one.
"Sonya, wait — we'll fit everything into these," said Natasha.
"You can't, miss — we've already tried," said the butler's assistant.
"No, hold on, please."
And Natasha began rapidly taking out the paper-wrapped dishes and plates from the case.
"The dishes should go in here, among the carpets," she said.
"It would be a miracle if we could get the carpets alone into three cases," said the butler's assistant.

"Just wait, please!" And Natasha began quickly and deftly sorting things. "These aren't needed," she said, setting aside some Kiev-ware plates. "These, yes — these go among the carpets," she said, referring to the Saxony china.
"Don't, Natasha! Leave it — we'll manage!" Sonya urged reproachfully.
"What a young lady!" the major-domo remarked.

But Natasha refused to give in. She emptied everything out and started repacking from scratch, deciding that the cheaper Russian carpets and unnecessary crockery shouldn't be taken at all. When everything had been removed from the cases and repacking began, it turned out that with the less valuable items rejected, the important ones actually did fit into the two cases. Only the lid of the carpet case wouldn't close. A few more items could have been taken out, but Natasha insisted on doing it her way. She packed, repacked, pressed, enlisted the butler's assistant and Petya — whom she'd drafted into the operation — to lean on the lid, and pushed desperately herself.
"That's enough, Natasha," said Sonya. "I see you were right, but just take out the top one."
"I won't!" cried Natasha, holding back with one hand the hair that hung over her sweating face while pressing down the carpets with the other. "Press now, Petya! Press, Vasilich — push hard!"

The carpets yielded and the lid closed. Natasha clapped her hands and screamed with delight, and tears fell from her eyes. But this lasted only a moment. She immediately set to work again, and now they trusted her completely. The count wasn't even angry when told Natasha had countermanded one of his orders, and the servants now came to her to ask whether a cart was loaded enough and whether it could be roped up. Thanks to Natasha's direction, the work went swiftly — unnecessary things were left behind and the most valuable items packed as tightly as possible.
But however hard they all worked late into the night, they couldn't get everything packed. The countess had fallen asleep, and the count, putting off departure until the next morning, went to bed.
Sonya and Natasha slept in the sitting room without undressing.

That night another wounded man was brought down the Povarskaya, and Mavra Kuzminichna, standing at the gate, had him brought into the Rostovs' yard. She judged he must be a very important person. He was being carried in a carriage with a raised hood, completely covered by a traveling blanket. On the box beside the driver sat a dignified old attendant. A doctor and two soldiers followed in a cart.
"Please come in here. The family is leaving and the whole house will be empty," the old woman said to the attendant.
"Well, perhaps," he said with a sigh. "We don't expect to get him home alive. We have our own house in Moscow, but it's a long way from here and nobody's living in it."
"Please, do us the honor — there's plenty of everything in the master's house. Come in," said Mavra Kuzminichna. "Is he very ill?" she asked.
The attendant made a hopeless gesture.
"We don't expect to get him home. We'll have to ask the doctor."
And the old servant climbed down from the box and went to the cart.
"All right," said the doctor.
The old servant returned to the carriage, looked inside, shook his head sadly, told the driver to turn into the yard, and stopped beside Mavra Kuzminichna.
"Lord Jesus Christ!" she murmured.
She invited them to bring the wounded man inside.
"The family won't mind..." she said.
But they had to avoid carrying him upstairs, so they put him in the wing — in the room that had been Madame Schoss's.
This wounded man was Prince Andrew Bolkonsky.

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: Before two o'clock the Rostovs' four carriages, fully packed and with horses harnessed, stood at the front door. One by one the carts carrying wounded men had moved out of the yard.

The carriage in which Prince Andrew was being transported caught Sonya's attention as it passed the front porch. She was arranging a seat for the countess in the huge, high coach at the entrance, with the help of a maid.
"Whose carriage is that?" she asked, leaning out of the window.
"Didn't you know, miss?" the maid replied. "The wounded prince — he spent the night in our house and is traveling with us."
"But who is he? What's his name?"
"It's our former intended — Prince Bolkonsky himself! They say he's dying," the maid replied with a sigh.

Sonya jumped out of the coach and ran to the countess. The countess, exhausted and already dressed in her shawl and bonnet for the journey, was pacing the drawing room, waiting for the household to assemble for the customary silent prayer before departure. Natasha was not in the room.
"Mama," said Sonya, "Prince Andrew is here — mortally wounded. He's going with us."
The countess opened her eyes in alarm and, seizing Sonya's arm, looked around.
"Natasha?" she whispered.

At that moment, the news had only one meaning for both of them. They knew their Natasha, and their alarm about what would happen if she learned this news overwhelmed any sympathy for the man they both liked.
"Natasha doesn't know yet, but he's going with us," said Sonya.
"You say he's dying?"
Sonya nodded.
The countess put her arms around Sonya and began to cry.
"The ways of God are beyond our understanding!" she thought, sensing that the Almighty Hand — until now unseen — was becoming visible in all that was happening.
"Well, Mama? Everything's ready. What's wrong?" asked Natasha, running into the room with an animated face.
"Nothing," the countess replied. "If everything's ready, let's go."
And the countess bent over her handbag to hide her troubled face. Sonya embraced Natasha and kissed her.
Natasha looked at her questioningly.
"What is it? What's happened?"
"Nothing... no..."
"Something bad for me? What is it?" Natasha persisted, with her quick intuition.

Sonya sighed and gave no reply. The count, Petya, Madame Schoss, Mavra Kuzminichna, and Vasilich came into the drawing room, and having closed the doors, they all sat down and remained for several moments in silence, not looking at one another.

The count was the first to stand. With a loud sigh he crossed himself before the icon. Everyone did the same. Then the count embraced Mavra Kuzminichna and Vasilich, who were staying in Moscow, and while they caught at his hand and kissed his shoulder, he patted their backs lightly with vaguely affectionate, comforting words. The countess went to the oratory, where Sonya found her on her knees before the icons left hanging here and there on the walls. (The most precious ones, carrying family traditions, were being taken along.)
In the porch and yard, the men Petya had armed with swords and daggers — trousers tucked into high boots, belts and straps tightened — were taking leave of those remaining behind.

As always happens at a departure, much had been forgotten or put in the wrong place, and for a long time two servants stood on either side of the open door and the carriage steps, waiting to help the countess in, while maids rushed back and forth between the house and the carriages with cushions and bundles.
"They always forget everything!" said the countess. "Don't you know I can't sit like that?"
And Dunyasha, clenching her teeth, saying nothing but with an aggrieved look, hurried into the coach to rearrange the seat.
"Oh, these servants!" said the count, shaking his head.

Efim, the old coachman — the only one the countess trusted to drive her — sat perched high on the box without so much as glancing back at what was going on behind him. From thirty years' experience he knew it would be a while yet before the command "Off, in God's name!" was given, and he knew that even after it was said he'd be stopped once or twice to send back for something forgotten, and even after that the countess herself would lean out the window and beg him, for the love of heaven, to drive carefully down the hill. He knew all this and so waited calmly — more patiently than the horses, especially the near one, the chestnut Falcon, who pawed the ground and champed his bit. At last everyone was seated, the steps folded up, the door shut, somebody sent for a forgotten travel case, and the countess leaned out to say what she had to say. Then Efim deliberately removed his hat and began crossing himself. The postilion and all the other servants did the same. "Off, in God's name!" said Efim, putting his hat back on. "Let's go!" The postilion started the horses, the off-side horse tugged at his collar, the tall springs creaked, and the coach body swayed. The footman leaped onto the box of the moving coach, which jolted as it passed through the gate onto the uneven road. The other vehicles jolted behind it in turn, and the procession moved up the street. In the carriages, the coach, and the phaeton, everyone crossed themselves as they passed the church across from the house. Those staying in Moscow walked alongside the vehicles, seeing the travelers off.

Rarely had Natasha felt such joy as now, sitting in the carriage beside the countess and gazing at the slowly receding walls of forsaken, agitated Moscow. Occasionally she leaned out the window and looked back, then forward at the long train of wounded ahead. Almost at the head of the column she could see the raised hood of Prince Andrew's carriage. She didn't know who was in it, but each time she looked at the procession, her eyes sought that carriage. She knew it was right in front.

In Kudrino, from the Nikitsky, Presnya, and Podnovinsky streets, several other trains of vehicles like the Rostovs' joined them, and as they moved along the Sadovaya Street, the carriages and carts formed two rows abreast.
As they rounded the Sukharev water tower, Natasha — who was attentively and alertly studying everyone they passed — suddenly cried out in joyful surprise:
"Oh my! Mama, Sonya, look — it's him!"
"Who? Who?"

"Look! Yes, I swear it's Bezukhov!" said Natasha, sticking her head out the window and staring at a tall, heavyset man in a coachman's long coat, who from his walk and movements was obviously a gentleman in disguise. He was passing under the arch of the Sukharev tower accompanied by a small, sallow-faced, beardless old man in a rough coat.
"Yes, it really is Bezukhov, in a coachman's coat, with a funny-looking old man. Really!" said Natasha. "Look, look!"
"No, it's not him. How can you say such nonsense?"
"Mama!" Natasha screamed. "I'll stake my head it's him! I swear! Stop! Stop!" she cried to the coachman.
But the coachman couldn't stop — more carts and carriages were pouring from Meshchanskaya Street, and the Rostovs were being shouted at to move along and not block the road.

In fact, though now much farther away than before, the whole Rostov family did see Pierre — or someone extraordinarily like him — in a coachman's coat, walking down the street with bowed head and a serious face beside a small, beardless old man who looked like a footman. The old man noticed a face staring at them from the carriage window and, respectfully touching Pierre's elbow, said something to him and pointed at the carriage. Pierre, clearly lost in thought, couldn't understand at first. But when he grasped what was said and looked where the old man pointed, he recognized Natasha, and following his first impulse, stepped quickly toward the coach. But after a dozen paces he seemed to remember something and stopped.
Natasha's face, leaning from the window, beamed with playful kindness.
"Peter Kirilych! Come here! We've recognized you! This is wonderful!" she cried, holding out her hand. "What are you doing? Why are you dressed like this?"
Pierre took her outstretched hand and kissed it awkwardly, walking alongside while the coach kept moving.
"What's the matter, Count?" asked the countess in a surprised, sympathetic tone.
"What? What? Why? Don't ask me," said Pierre, and he glanced at Natasha, whose radiant, happy expression — which he sensed without directly looking at her — filled him with enchantment.
"Are you staying in Moscow, then?"
Pierre hesitated.
"In Moscow?" he said questioningly. "Yes, in Moscow. Goodbye!"
"Oh, if only I were a man, I'd definitely stay with you. How wonderful!" said Natasha. "Mama, if you'll let me, I'll stay!"
Pierre looked at Natasha absently and was about to say something, but the countess interrupted.
"You were in the battle, we heard."
"Yes, I was," Pierre answered. "There'll be another battle tomorrow..." he began, but Natasha cut him off.
"But what's the matter with you, Count? You're not yourself..."
"Oh, don't ask me, don't ask me! I don't know myself. Tomorrow... But no! Goodbye — goodbye!" he murmured. "What a terrible time!" And falling behind the carriage, he stepped onto the sidewalk.
Natasha continued leaning out the window for a long time, beaming at him with her kind, slightly teasing, happy smile.

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: For the past two days, since leaving home, Pierre had been living in the empty house of his late benefactor, Bazdeev. This is how it came about.

When he woke up on the morning after his return to Moscow and his meeting with Count Rostopchin, he couldn't at first figure out where he was or what was expected of him. When told that among the people waiting for him in the reception room was a Frenchman who had brought a letter from his wife, Countess Helene, he was suddenly overcome by that feeling of confusion and hopelessness to which he was prone. He felt that everything was finished, everything in chaos, everything crumbling — nobody was right or wrong, the future held nothing, and there was no way out. Smiling awkwardly and muttering to himself, he first sat down on the sofa in a posture of despair, then got up, went to the reception room door, peeked through the crack, came back waving his arms, and picked up a book. His major-domo came in again to say that the Frenchman who'd brought the letter from the countess was very eager to see him, if only for a minute, and that someone from Bazdeev's widow had come asking Pierre to take charge of her late husband's books, as she was leaving for the country.
"Oh, yes — in a moment. Wait... or no! No, of course... go and tell him I'll come directly," Pierre said to the major-domo.

But as soon as the man left, Pierre grabbed his hat from the table and went out of the study through the other door. No one was in the hallway. He walked its full length to the stairs and, frowning and rubbing his forehead with both hands, went down to the first landing. The hall porter was standing at the front door. From the landing where Pierre stood, a second staircase led to the back entrance. He went down it and out into the yard. No one had seen him. But some carriages were waiting, and the moment Pierre stepped through the gate, the coachmen and the yard porter spotted him and raised their caps. Feeling observed, Pierre acted like an ostrich that hides its head in a bush to avoid being seen — he hung his head and, quickening his pace, hurried down the street.
Of all the matters awaiting him that day, sorting through Joseph Bazdeev's books and papers struck Pierre as the most necessary.
He hailed the first cab he found and told the driver to go to the Patriarch's Ponds, where the widow Bazdeev's house was.

Constantly turning around to look at the loaded carts making their way from every direction out of Moscow, and balancing his bulky body so as not to slide out of the rickety old vehicle, Pierre — feeling the joyful relief of a boy escaping school — began chatting with his driver.
The driver told him arms were being distributed at the Kremlin, and that tomorrow everyone would be sent out beyond the Three Hills gates where a great battle would take place.

Having reached the Patriarch's Ponds, Pierre found the Bazdeev house, where he hadn't been in a long time. He went up to the gate. Gerasim — that sallow, beardless old man Pierre had seen at Torzhok five years earlier with Joseph Bazdeev — came out in answer to his knock.
"Is the mistress home?" asked Pierre.
"Due to the present situation, Sophia Danilovna has gone with the children to the Torzhok estate, your excellency."
"I'll come in anyway — I need to look through the books," said Pierre.
"Please, step in. Makar Alexeevich — the brother of my late master, may the kingdom of heaven be his — has stayed here, but he's in a poor state, as you know," said the old servant.
Pierre knew that Makar Alexeevich was Joseph Bazdeev's half-mad brother and a heavy drinker.
"Yes, yes, I know. Let's go in..." Pierre said, and he entered the house.
A tall, bald-headed old man with a red nose, wearing a dressing gown and galoshes on his bare feet, stood in the anteroom. Seeing Pierre, he muttered something angry and shuffled away down the hall.

"He was once a very clever man, but he's grown quite feeble now, as your honor can see," said Gerasim. "Will you come into the study?" Pierre nodded. "It's been kept sealed up just as it was, but Sophia Danilovna gave orders that if anyone came from you, they were to have the books."
Pierre went into the gloomy study he had once entered with such trepidation during his benefactor's lifetime. The room, dusty and untouched since Joseph Bazdeev's death, was gloomier than ever.

Gerasim opened one of the shutters and left the room on tiptoe. Pierre went around the study, approached the cupboard where the manuscripts were kept, and took out what had once been the most sacred treasure of the order — the authentic Scottish Acts with Bazdeev's notes and commentaries. He sat down at the dusty desk, laid the manuscripts before him, opened them, closed them, then pushed them away, and resting his head on his hand, sank into thought.
Gerasim peeked cautiously into the study several times and saw Pierre always sitting in the same position.
More than two hours passed, and Gerasim took the liberty of making a slight noise at the door to get his attention, but Pierre didn't hear him.
"Should the cab be dismissed, your honor?"

"Oh, yes!" said Pierre, rousing himself and jumping up. "Listen," he added, taking Gerasim by a button of his coat and looking down at the old man with moist, shining, ecstatic eyes. "Listen — do you know there's going to be a battle tomorrow?"
"So we've heard," the man replied.
"I beg you not to tell anyone who I am, and to do what I ask."
"Yes, your excellency," Gerasim replied. "Will you have something to eat?"
"No, but I need something else. I need peasant clothes and a pistol," said Pierre, unexpectedly blushing.
"Yes, your excellency," said Gerasim after a moment's thought.
Pierre spent the rest of the day alone in his benefactor's study, and Gerasim heard him pacing restlessly from corner to corner, talking to himself. He spent the night on a bed made up for him there.

Gerasim, as a servant who had seen many strange things in his time, accepted Pierre's taking up residence without surprise and seemed pleased to have someone to wait on. That same evening — without even asking what they were for — he procured a coachman's coat and cap for Pierre and promised to get the pistol the next day. Makar Alexeevich came shuffling in his galoshes to the door twice that evening, stopping to peer ingratiatingly at Pierre. But as soon as Pierre turned toward him, he wrapped his dressing gown around himself with a shamefaced, angry look and hurried away. It was when Pierre — wearing the coachman's coat Gerasim had obtained and disinfected by steaming — was on his way with the old man to buy the pistol at the Sukharev market that he encountered the Rostovs.

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: Kutuzov's order to retreat through Moscow to the Ryazan road was issued on the night of September 1.

The first troops set out at once, marching slowly and steadily through the night without haste. At daybreak, however, those approaching the city at the Dorogomilov bridge found masses of soldiers crowding and rushing across the bridge ahead of them, jamming the streets and alleys on the far side, while endless columns bore down from behind. An unreasoning panic and urgency overcame them all. They surged forward to the bridge, onto it, and toward the fords and boats. Kutuzov himself had taken a detour through side streets to the other side of Moscow.
By ten in the morning of September 2, only the rear guard remained in the Dorogomilov district, with plenty of room. The main army was on the other side of Moscow or already beyond it.

At that very hour — ten in the morning of September 2 — Napoleon was standing among his troops on Poklonny Hill, surveying the panorama spread before him. From August 26 to September 2 — from the Battle of Borodino to the French entry into Moscow — during that whole stirring, memorable week, there had been the kind of extraordinary autumn weather that always comes as a surprise: when the sun hangs low and gives more warmth than in spring, when everything shines so brightly in the rare clear air that it stings the eyes, when the lungs feel strengthened and refreshed by the fragrant autumn air, when even the nights are warm, and when from those dark warm skies golden stars constantly startle and delight by falling.
At ten on the morning of September 2, this weather still held.

The brightness of the morning was magical. Moscow, seen from Poklonny Hill, lay spaciously spread out with its river, gardens, and churches, and seemed to be living its usual life, its domes glittering like stars in the sunlight.

The view of the strange city with its unfamiliar architecture filled Napoleon with the rather envious and uneasy curiosity men feel when encountering a foreign way of life that knows nothing of them. This city was clearly alive with the full force of its own existence. By those indefinable signs that even at a distance distinguish a living body from a dead one, Napoleon sensed from Poklonny Hill the throb of life in the city and felt, as it were, the breathing of that great and beautiful body.

Every Russian looking at Moscow feels her to be a mother; every foreigner who sees her, even without knowing her significance as the mother city, must sense her feminine character. And Napoleon felt it.

"That Asian city of countless churches — holy Moscow! Here it is at last, that famous city. It was high time," he said, and dismounting, he ordered a map of Moscow spread before him and summoned his interpreter, Lelorgne d'Ideville.
* "That Asian city of countless churches — holy Moscow! Here it is at last, that famous city. It was high time."

"A town captured by the enemy is like a maiden who has lost her honor," he thought (he had said as much to Tuchkov at Smolensk). From that vantage point he gazed at the Eastern beauty he hadn't seen before. It seemed strange that his long-held wish, which had seemed unattainable, was at last realized. In the clear morning light he looked from the city to the map and back again, and the certainty of possessing it both excited and awed him.

"But could it have been otherwise?" he thought. "Here is this capital at my feet. Where is Alexander now, and what is he thinking? A strange, beautiful, majestic city — and a strange and majestic moment! In what light must I appear to them!" he reflected, thinking of his troops. "Here she is — the reward for all those fainthearted men," he mused, glancing at his entourage and the approaching troops. "One word from me, one movement of my hand, and that ancient capital of the Tsars would perish. But my clemency is always ready to descend upon the vanquished. I must be magnanimous and truly great. But no — it can't be true that I'm in Moscow," he suddenly thought. "Yet here she lies at my feet, with her golden domes and crosses gleaming in the sun. But I shall spare her. On the ancient monuments of barbarism and despotism I shall inscribe great words of justice and mercy. This is what Alexander will feel most keenly — I know him." (It seemed to Napoleon that the chief significance of events lay in his personal rivalry with Alexander.) "From the heights of the Kremlin — yes, there it is — I shall give them just laws. I shall teach them what true civilization means. I shall make generations of boyars remember their conqueror with love. I shall tell the delegation that I did not and do not wish for war, that I have fought only against the false policy of their court; that I love and respect Alexander and that in Moscow I shall accept peace terms worthy of myself and my peoples. 'Boyars,' I shall say to them, 'I do not desire war. I desire the peace and welfare of all my subjects.' However, I know their presence will inspire me, and I shall speak as I always do — clearly, impressively, and majestically. But can it really be true that I'm in Moscow? Yes, there she lies."
"Bring the boyars to me," he said to his entourage.
* "Bring the boyars to me."
A general with a brilliant retinue galloped off at once to fetch the boyars.

Two hours passed. Napoleon had lunched and was standing again in the same spot on Poklonny Hill, waiting for the delegation. His speech to the boyars had already taken definite shape in his imagination. That speech was full of dignity and grandeur as Napoleon understood them.

He was carried away by the tone of magnanimity he planned to adopt toward Moscow. In his mind he set dates for assemblies at the Tsar's palace where Russian dignitaries and his own people would mingle. He mentally appointed a governor, one who would win the people's hearts. Knowing there were many charitable institutions in Moscow, he decided he would shower them all with favors. He thought that just as in Africa he had worn a burnoose and sat in a mosque, so in Moscow he must be beneficent like the Tsars. And to touch the hearts of the Russians — and being, like all Frenchmen, unable to imagine anything sentimental without a reference to his dear, tender, poor mother — he decided to place an inscription on every institution: "Dedicated to my dear mother."
